second_order: playing and picking apart a Salvy trade prank
theme_note: These codes hold together as the room's own April Fools practice: one person stages a fake trade while others expose it, curse it, propose more believable versions, compare past pranks, or finally credit the joke. What varies is whether participants are making, detecting, rejecting, improving, or conceding the prank; none of it concerns the canvas.

second_order: calling people in to make a Royals mark
theme_note: The shared practice is recruiting and joining collective Royals work: calls for a KC logo or mark are answered by offers, participation, and renewed encouragement. The calls vary from an early blue-corner proposal to the main 'collective dongs' appeal, a removed-body title, and persistence once a crown is visible.

second_order: finding the spot and building the crown together
theme_note: These codes coordinate the hands-on build by choosing a time and crown, giving a bottom pixel or direction, finding and restarting at locations, checking whether work continues, staying overnight, and reporting progress. What varies is orientation, timing, persistence, and whether participants report stopping or continuing.

second_order: explaining r/place to people catching up
theme_note: The practice is making the event understandable to people who do not know what organizers mean or cannot yet participate: members explain the canvas, teamwork, device difficulty, and access. Later questions vary the practice by asking whether it ended and whether it was an April Fools event.

second_order: running scripts and extra accounts to keep placing
theme_note: These passages multiply and sustain placements through scripts, several accounts, overnight or workplace running, visibility for instructions, and troubleshooting. Participants vary in account count, device limits, success, and the help needed to get the script working.

second_order: working out room with neighboring pictures
theme_note: The common practice is dealing with overlapping claims on canvas space: participants warn, resist, request movement, offer reciprocal help, relocate, propose alliances, apologize, and plan repairs. What varies is whether the stance is competitive, accommodating, or cooperative, and whether an agreement lasts long enough to act on.

second_order: deciding whether the finish counted as a win
theme_note: These codes assess the community's result and credit the people behind it: participants mourn the end, call the effort failure or victory, refresh and revise their view, celebrate a photo finish, thank the group, or praise its organizers. What varies is the standard used—completeness, beauty, final-canvas presence, comparison with larger groups, or simple group effort—and critics are directly rebuffed.

second_order: sharing and looking through the finished canvas
theme_note: This later-slice practice consists of circulating the full picture, helping someone locate the Royals logo, sharing a time lapse, and reacting to other pictures visible in the completed canvas. What varies is whether people are locating their own work, marveling at the whole project, or pointing out other communities' images.

second_order: sending bored people to r/place for stupid amusement
theme_note: This single late code points people from ordinary pregame chat to r/place as amusement; it neither recruits the KC logo build nor explains the event, so it belongs with no other practice.
